stanley.summary: Vancouver's living room: seawall, totem poles, old forest, and three beaches.
stanley.body: The park is the forested peninsula on the north side of downtown. The seawall is about nine kilometres, flat enough to walk, run, cycle, or push a stroller. Totem poles, Lost Lagoon, Beaver Lake, and Second and Third Beaches are inside. The aquarium, miniature train, and horse-drawn tour cost extra. Weekend afternoons fill the parking lots, so come early or take the bus or a bike. The water is cooler than downtown.
tips: For sunset, walk out the south end to English Bay.
Keep the stroller on the seawall. Forest paths have roots and hills.

aquarium.summary: The most reliable indoor stop on a wet day, with sea otters, jellyfish, and dolphins.
aquarium.body: The aquarium is inside Stanley Park and is the region's fullest marine museum. Toddlers like the touch pool and jellyfish. School-age children usually stop at the otters. Tickets are not cheap, so save it for rain, cold, or heat. There is a cafe, but a picnic on the seawall costs less. Strollers fit inside.
tips: Ticket prices depend on age. Check the site that day.
Afternoons are quieter than tour-group mornings.

science-world.summary: A hands-on science centre where school-age children rarely say they are bored.
science-world.body: The silver dome sits at the end of False Creek, with the SkyTrain station at the door. Galleries cover the body, water, and light, and there is a wet area for younger children, so bring a change of clothes. The dome theatre is a separate ticket. The seawall outside continues toward Olympic Village.
tips: A membership pays off if you will come two or three times a year.
You can skip the wet area and still fill the day.

granville.summary: A covered public market, a kids' market, and a shore where you can watch boats.
granville.body: Granville Island used to be industrial. Now it is a market, workshops, and buskers. You can buy fruit, baked goods, and hot food under a roof. The Kids Market is a building of small shops and play. You still walk outside between buildings. Weekend noon is crowded, and the parking garage fills.
tips: The little ferries charge by route, and children like the bow.
After the market, walk the island's boardwalk.

vandusen.summary: A large city garden with a maze, a children's garden, and October colour.
vandusen.body: VanDusen has woods, a lake, and gardens grouped by plant type. Children head for the hedge maze and the children's garden. Spring is rhododendrons, October is leaves, and December is the light festival, which needs a separate evening ticket. The conservatory is only a short shelter from rain.
tips: Book the Festival of Lights ahead in December.
Queen Elizabeth Park is close enough to pair on the same day.

qepark.summary: A former quarry turned into gardens, with the city and the North Shore mountains from the top.
qepark.body: The park sits on a small hill. The old quarry is now terraced gardens. From the top you can see both the water and the mountains. Bloedel Conservatory needs a small extra ticket. Tropical plants and koi are the reward when legs are tired. The park itself is free. April, May, and October have the best colour.
tips: The conservatory ticket is separate from the park.
The summit is windier than the gardens below.

sun-yat-sen.summary: A classical Chinese garden in Chinatown, with white walls, a pond, and framed views.
sun-yat-sen.body: This is one of the few classical Chinese gardens downtown. The paid garden includes a talk that explains each window. The public park next door is free if you only want a look from outside. It is small, so pair it with a Chinatown walk rather than expecting it to use up a high-energy afternoon. Ask children not to climb the rocks or throw things in the pond.
tips: The public park is free. The classical garden charges admission.
Chinese-language tours are not every day. Check the site.

chinatown.summary: The gate, cafes, bakeries, and the Chinese Canadian Museum.
chinatown.body: Vancouver's Chinatown is one of the oldest in North America. Pender Street has the gate, old association buildings, and bakeries that are still open. The Chinese Canadian Museum is in this neighbourhood. Check its hours and tickets. The street itself is free. It suits children who can walk and listen, especially during a flower market or lion dance.
tips: Pair it with the Chinese garden and Gastown in one half day.
If the museum is closed, sit down at a bakery instead.

gastown.summary: The steam clock marks the hour. Pair it with Canada Place and the seawall.
gastown.body: Gastown is the old downtown, with cobblestones and the steam clock. The clock does a small show about every quarter hour and whistles on the hour, so you do not need to wait a full hour. The street is free. Restaurants nearby are pricey. Evenings are more about bars, so bring children in the daytime. The lights in December are worth seeing.
tips: The sidewalk by the clock is narrow. Watch and move on.
From here you can walk the seawall into Stanley Park without a ticket.

moa.summary: A glass hall of Northwest Coast poles, and a strong rainy-day choice.
moa.body: The Museum of Anthropology is at the ocean end of the University of British Columbia. The Great Hall looks out through glass to the water. The collection is mainly Northwest Coast Indigenous poles, houses, and masks, plus objects from elsewhere. Children may not read every label, but the carvings are large enough to hold them. Thursday evenings sometimes run late or cost less. Check the site. The lawn outside is windy.
tips: Very young children may find the galleries too quiet. Science World is the easier indoor choice.
The Beaty Biodiversity Museum is on the same campus.

beaty.summary: A blue whale skeleton hangs from the ceiling. That is the reason to come.
beaty.body: This is the university's natural history museum. The blue whale is the first thing you see, followed by shells, fossils, fish, and insects. It is smaller and quieter than Science World, and it suits school-age children who ask questions. Admission is usually modest. With the Museum of Anthropology and Pacific Spirit Park it can make a UBC day, which is too much for a toddler.
tips: The whale is the photo. The drawer specimens go faster.
Campus parking is zoned. Read the signs.

space-centre.summary: A planetarium and space exhibits for children who like stars and rockets.
space-centre.body: The space centre is in Vanier Park in Kitsilano. The star show is the highlight. Children sit in tilted seats and watch the sky. Check the length if a child is afraid of the dark or gets dizzy. The Maritime Museum and a kite lawn are next door, so a dry hour can be paired with grass.
tips: Check the next star-show time as soon as you enter.
You do not have to do the Maritime Museum the same day.

english-bay.summary: A downtown sunset, freighters, and a beach where you can sit.
english-bay.body: English Bay is just south of Stanley Park and is the easiest downtown beach to reach. Lifeguards are on duty in summer swimming hours. In October it is better for walking, watching ships, and takeout. The summer fireworks are watched from here, and the crowd is huge. An ordinary evening is the comfortable version. Fine sand can sink stroller wheels.
tips: On fireworks night, transit beats driving.
Denman Street next door has ice cream and simple food.

kits.summary: A city beach plus a saltwater pool that opens only in summer.
kits.body: Kitsilano Beach faces English Bay and has finer sand than many city beaches. The large saltwater pool usually runs from May to September. In other months this is a walk and a sand play, not a swim. There is a playground beside the beach. Summer weekends make parking hard. The seaside greenway is the sensible way to arrive by bike. The water is colder than it looks when the wind is up.
tips: Assume the pool is closed in October unless the park board says otherwise.
Jericho Beach, to the west, is wider and quieter.

pacific-spirit.summary: Coastal forest beside the university, dense with trails and quiet in the morning.
pacific-spirit.body: This regional park wraps the university and is the easiest temperate rainforest to enter from the city. Some trails are easy and some are not. A stroller belongs only on a few wide gravel paths. Pick a short loop that returns to the same entrance. After rain it is muddy. Cell service can be weak, so look at a map before you start.
tips: Flatter trails such as Clinton are the family choice.
The campus museums are the rainy backup.

flyover.summary: A suspended ride over Canadian scenery. About half an hour of thrill on a rainy day.
flyover.body: FlyOver Canada is inside Canada Place. Seats hang in front of a huge screen and simulate flight, with wind, mist, and motion. With the wait, plan about an hour. Skip it if someone gets motion sick or hates heights. Very young children usually should not go. Afterward, the outdoor walkway at Canada Place is free and looks over cruise ships and seaplanes.
tips: Read the height and age notes on the ticket page.
The steam clock in Gastown fits the same short outing.

lookout.summary: An elevator to a downtown viewpoint that puts the sea, the mountains, and the streets in one glance.
lookout.body: The lookout is on the Harbour Centre tower, and the elevator is already the part children like. On a clear day you can see the North Shore snow, the direction of the Fraser, and the green of Stanley Park. The glass floor is optional. You do not need to stay long. If the mountains have disappeared into low cloud, the windows will be white.
tips: Some tickets allow re-entry the same day. Read the ticket.
If the cloud is low, come another day.

playland.summary: Roller coasters and rides, busiest in summer and during the Pacific National Exhibition.
playland.body: Playland is in the PNE grounds in East Vancouver. It runs from spring into early fall, and the August fair is the busiest, with fireworks and stalls. There is a children's area for riders who are not tall enough, and teens head for the wooden coaster. Most rides are outside. Do not go in a real downpour. A wristband day is expensive for a family. Eat before you enter.
tips: The calendar changes every year. In October, check the site before you drive.
Nervous children can stay in the small-ride area.

false-creek.summary: A flat seawall with the city on one side and small boats on the other.
false-creek.body: The False Creek seawall links Science World, Olympic Village, and the shore opposite Granville Island. It is almost level, which makes it the easiest piece of city waterfront for a stroller or a balance bike. You will see houseboats and ferries. Washrooms are at Science World and the village, not in the middle.
tips: The bike path and the walking path are separate. Keep children to the right.
Olympic Village is the place to find a washroom and a cafe.

commercial.summary: Ice cream, pizza, and small parks along a street that feels lived in.
commercial.body: Commercial Drive is the easiest eat-and-walk street on the east side. There is ice cream, pizza, and small restaurants, and someone is often playing on the sidewalk on weekends. The street is not a sight on its own. It works because children have a concrete goal. A few small parks let toddlers run. Use timed parking on the side streets.
tips: Saturday sidewalks are full. Go slowly with a stroller.
Trout Lake is close if you want grass as well.

garry.summary: Watch fishing boats and planes, on a lawn big enough for a kite.
garry.body: Garry Point is the west end of Steveston, with water on three sides. Fishing boats pass close, and on a clear day you can see planes landing at the Richmond airport. The grass suits kites and picnics, and the wind is usually stronger than downtown. There is not much playground equipment. Toddlers are happy running and watching boats. Sunsets are good. Washrooms are on the village side.
tips: Hats need a strap.
Walk back along the boardwalk for fish and chips. You do not need the car.

steveston.summary: Fish and chips, a boardwalk, candy, and a dock that still lands fish.
steveston.body: Steveston is a working harbour, not a fake old street. Bayview Street has fish-and-chips shops, and weekends mean a wait. You can see boats and, sometimes, sea lions. Do not wait all day for the sea lions. There is a candy shop and a bookstore. The cannery and the shipyard are at either end of the village and both are walkable. Use the public lots.
tips: If the shop has no seats, take the food to Garry Point.
Sea lions are a bonus, not a guarantee.

cannery.summary: A cannery that still has its production line, and the story of how salmon was canned.
cannery.body: The cannery is a national historic site on the dock. Inside you can see the old line and fishery exhibits, often with something to touch. It is small, which makes it the indoor piece of a Steveston half day. Winter hours shrink, and it may not open every day. Admission is usually modest.
tips: Do not drive here on its own. Pair it with the shipyard and the village.
Check the Parks Canada calendar in winter.

britannia.summary: An old shipyard and workers' housing on the river. The grounds are free, and the buildings open by season.
britannia.body: The shipyard stretches along the Steveston channel, with a boat shed and Chinese and Japanese bunkhouses. It tells the cannery and shipbuilding story, including Indigenous, Chinese, and Japanese Canadian workers. You can walk the outside from morning to evening. Indoor buildings often open only on weekends in late fall and winter. The main path works for a stroller. There is a maritime festival around August.
tips: If the buildings are shut, the river and the wooden boats are still the visit.
High tide or repairs can close a building. Read the sign.

temple.summary: A free Chinese Buddhist garden, with gold tiles, white railings, and a quiet courtyard.
temple.body: The International Buddhist Temple is free and runs on donations. The main hall is ornate, and the courtyard has rocks, water, and covered walks. Take shoes off in the hall, cover shoulders, and take hats off. Ask children not to run or touch offerings. You may photograph the courtyard. Follow the signs inside the hall. Weekends and Lunar New Year are busy.
tips: There is no cafe. Eat in Steveston or at Aberdeen.
This is a temple, not a playground. Half an hour to an hour is enough.

night-market.summary: A summer-night snack city, open from about April to September.
night-market.body: The Richmond Night Market is on River Road, a block from Bridgeport Station. It usually runs Friday to Sunday evenings from late April to mid or late September, sometimes on holiday Mondays. Admission is low, and young children and seniors are often free. The food is the real cost. Smoke, music, and crowds can overwhelm a small child. A stroller works on the main aisle and struggles between stalls. Do not make a special trip from October until the next spring.
tips: The 2026 season ended on September 20. The next one waits until April.
There is sometimes a late-night price after 10 p.m. Check that year's site.

iona.summary: Planes pass just overhead, and a long jetty walks out into the sea.
iona.body: Iona is at the north end of the airport runway. Jets come in low, which is the thrill. A long jetty reaches into the strait. It is windy and has almost no shade. The wetland beside it is for birds. Bring food and water. This is not a swimming beach. Sunset in summer and birds in winter are both good. Midday sun is harsh.
tips: Hat, windbreaker, water. There is no shop on the jetty.
The noise is huge. Try a few minutes if a toddler is sensitive to sound.

richmond-nature.summary: A boardwalk through bog forest. Short, flat, and good for toddlers.
richmond-nature.body: This is a rare peat bog inside the city, with a boardwalk raised over the wetland. The loop is short, under an hour, and a stroller can take the main boards. The nature house sometimes opens, and the walk still works if it does not. Mosquitoes are busy in warm months. There is no ocean and no big playground. The point is that the highway is close and children will not get lost in a large forest.
tips: Boards are slippery after rain.
Aberdeen and the Olympic Oval are also in central Richmond if you want an easy day.

oval.summary: The indoor hall left by the Winter Olympics. You can skate, work out, or just look at the building.
oval.body: The Oval was the 2010 speed-skating venue and now offers public sports. Public skating, swimming, or climbing depends on that day's schedule. You cannot assume the ice is open because the door is. The wooden roof is worth seeing, and the river dyke outside is free. Treat it as a rainy backup and confirm the public session first.
tips: Skating usually needs a booked time. Do not assume you can walk onto the ice.
The river path outside is free. Activities inside are extra.

terra-nova.summary: Barns, a zip line, and river fields, like a farm fitted into the city.
terra-nova.body: Terra Nova has a red building, community gardens, a playground, and a short adventure course. You can see the Fraser. Markets happen some weekends, not every weekend. The ground is flat. There is no large restaurant, so picnic. The West Dyke links it with Steveston for bikes or feet.
tips: Ropes and zip lines depend on the day and on age. Wet wood is slippery.
Leave before the evening mosquitoes in high summer.

dyke.summary: A long straight path with fields on one side and the strait on the other.
dyke.body: The West Dyke is Richmond's western flood wall. The surface is flat and suits bikes and strollers. You can see planes, birds, and the direction of Vancouver Island. There is almost no shade and no shop, so bring water. The wind is strong. Walk or ride one piece. You do not have to do the whole length. Sunset is beautiful and colder.
tips: Most families bring their own bikes.
Stop at Garry Point or Terra Nova so the ride has a reason to pause.

aberdeen.summary: When it rains, come here: an Asian mall, a food court, and Yaohan next door.
aberdeen.body: Aberdeen Centre is on No. 3 Road, with the Canada Line station in the mall. The food court has noodles, dumplings, and dessert. Yaohan, next door, is another Asian department store with a busy food floor. This is not scenery. It is the simplest indoor plan for a rainy family weekend. The parkade circles on weekends. Stay for a meal and one loop, not a whole day.
tips: You do not have to cross a road from the Canada Line.
If the sky clears, go to the river. If it does not, this can be the whole outing.

bvm.summary: An old-time street, a carousel, and a seasonal Christmas village. Ordinary admission is free.
bvm.body: The museum is a made-up historic street beside Deer Lake. In summer it is open Tuesday to Sunday and closed Monday. Halloween and Christmas have evening events. The Christmas village charges admission. Regular entry is free. A carousel ride is about three dollars. In mid-October, before the haunted evenings, the street may be closed. Walk Deer Lake next door instead. The site is small, which suits toddlers.
tips: In 2026 the haunted village runs on the evenings of October 23 to 25 and October 30 to 31.
The Christmas village starts in late November. Check closed days.

deerlake.summary: A city lake, an art gallery, a playground, and the museum on the same loop.
deerlake.body: Deer Lake is Burnaby's easiest family walk. The shore path is flat, with a playground, picnics, and a small beach. The Burnaby Art Gallery occupies an old house and can be skipped without ruining the day. Small boats rent in summer. Wear life jackets. Fall colour is good along the shore. Do not try to do this lake, the village museum, and Burnaby Lake as one overpacked afternoon.
tips: Geese will go for food. Do not let a toddler run with a snack.
The gallery keeps shorter hours than the park.

burnabylake.summary: A boardwalk for turtles and waterbirds, and salmon in the creeks in fall.
burnabylake.body: Burnaby Lake is a regional park. The Piper Spit boardwalk reaches into the lake, and turtles and birds come close. The nature house has exhibits and washrooms and keeps shorter hours than the park. From September to November, side creeks can hold salmon. Ask staff which creek has fish that week. The full loop is too long for a stroller. The boardwalk section is enough.
tips: Do not feed the turtles or the birds.
On fish-season weekends, park properly. Do not block the road.

central-park.summary: Tall trees and a playground that can occupy children for a long time.
central-park.body: Central Park sits between the SkyTrain and Kingsway, and the woods are quiet once you are inside. The playground has been renewed and works for toddlers and school-age children. There are trails, tennis, and a small lake loop. Summer water play depends on the park notice. It is an easy afternoon when you do not want to drive into the mountains.
tips: The station exit crosses a road. Watch children.
Metropolis is one stop away if the rain starts.

metrotown.summary: One of the region's largest indoor malls. On a wet day, eating and walking stay under a roof.
metrotown.body: Metropolis at Metrotown is a shopping centre, not a view. It is on this map because a rainy Greater Vancouver weekend needs an indoor plan that does not require a debate: a food court, long corridors, and a SkyTrain station. Do not make it the high point of the day. If the sky clears, Central Park is nearby.
tips: Weekend parking circles. The SkyTrain is easier.
A mall is a poor place to burn energy. Use the park next door for that.

barnet.summary: Grass and a pier facing Burrard Inlet, with trains passing the edge.
barnet.body: Barnet is on Burnaby's north shore. There is a pier, picnic tables, and a small beach. Children like the trains on the park edge. The tracks are not a ride. Stay well away from them. The water is cold and most days are not for swimming. You can see the North Shore mountains. Facilities are simpler than a city beach.
tips: Explain the tracks before you let go of hands.
A frisbee or a kite is more realistic than a swim.

sfu.summary: A playground on the university hill, with Burrard Inlet below.
sfu.body: Simon Fraser University sits on Burnaby Mountain. The park on the east side has large wooden play structures, and the viewpoint looks over the inlet, the mountains, and the port. Clear days in September and October are especially sharp. You can walk through the academic quadrangle and then come back to the playground. It is colder up here than in the city. Use visitor parking and obey the lines.
tips: The playground is in Burnaby Mountain Park, not in the middle of the classrooms.
If the view is fogged in, the playground still works.

nikkei.summary: A museum about Japanese Canadians, with a Japanese garden beside it.
nikkei.body: The museum is modest. Exhibits cover immigration, the wartime forced uprooting, and the community that followed. It suits school-age children and teens who will listen. Toddlers will see too many panels. The Japanese garden next door is free to walk and is often the part younger children want to stay in. Hours are not all day, every day. Check the site.
tips: For a young child, the garden alone is a complete visit.
If the day needs running, go to Deer Lake instead.

confederation.summary: A large neighbourhood park, often with a miniature train on weekends.
confederation.body: Confederation Park has a playground, woods, and sports fields. The Burnaby Central Railway runs a small train through a short tunnel and over a small bridge. A ride is usually only a few dollars. The train does not run every day. Summer weekends and some holidays are the likely times. The park itself is free all year. Check whether the train is operating, or treat this as a good neighbourhood park.
tips: The train schedule is strongly seasonal. Trust the notice, not a rumour.
Toddlers can ride. Older children can use the playground.

bear-creek.summary: Surrey's all-in-one family park: gardens, a small train, a playground, and summer water.
bear-creek.body: Bear Creek is one of Surrey's most complete family parks. There are ornamental gardens, play equipment, and sports fields. Summer adds water play, and weekends often have a miniature train. Do not expect the train and the water in every season. The grounds are large, so a stroller helps. You can spend an afternoon here without buying a ticket. Parking is free and still tight in peak season.
tips: Look at the seasonal map first. Water and the train may be in different corners.
The gardens are for photos. Children's patience is at the playground.

crescent.summary: A real sand beach, with Blackie Spit beside it for watching birds.
crescent.body: Crescent Beach is in southwest Surrey. The sand is better than many river beaches, and it gets very wide at low tide. Summer is for sand and wading. The water is still cold. The village has small restaurants and ice cream. Blackie Spit, next door, is mudflat and grass. It is better for birds than for digging. The tide can cover the flat quickly.
tips: Use low tide for Blackie Spit and high tide for the sand.
White Rock pier is a short drive if you want both in one day.

tynehead.summary: In October and November, watch salmon jump at the hatchery ponds.
tynehead.body: Tynehead has forest trails and a salmon hatchery. In the run, fish crowd the ladder and the shallow creek, and children can see them at once. In other months it is a quiet forest park, still worth a walk, just without the fish. The main path suits a stroller. Side paths turn to mud. Watch from the platform. Do not let children onto wet rocks at the water.
tips: The run is roughly September to November. The peak depends on that year's rain.
You do not need this and the Capilano hatchery on the same day. Pick the closer one.

redwood.summary: Very tall trees, and a clearing with a treehouse story.
redwood.body: Redwood Park is known for its height. Two brothers once lived in the trees. The treehouse is gone and the forest remains. Trails are short, with picnic spots and play equipment. The canopy is beautiful in fall. Roots and slopes mean a stroller should stay on the main path. It works as a stop on the way to White Rock or the border.
tips: Wet roots are slippery.
There is no food. Bring snacks.

stewart.summary: An old farm on the river and a mudflat trail. Stewart House opens by season.
stewart.body: Elgin Heritage Park sits on the Nicomekl River and includes the 1880s Stewart farmhouse. The house has limited hours, mostly summer weekends. The park and river path are walkable at other times, with birds and boats. The grass suits toddlers. It is a slow visit, not a high-energy playground. Check the City of Surrey notice before you expect the house to be open.
tips: Walk the river even if the house is closed.
Crescent Beach is close. Plan one real meal, not two.

green-timbers.summary: A flat forest loop around a lake, right beside the highway.
green-timbers.body: Green Timbers is an old forest inside Surrey, with a lake in the middle and a relatively flat loop. It is easier than a mountain and more wooded than a mall. A stroller can take the lakeside path. Dirt sections soften after rain. There is no ocean. Use it as a one-hour outing, not as the whole destination.
tips: With toddlers, stay by the lake rather than taking the hill paths.
Make sure you can find the same parking lot on the way back.

peace-arch.summary: Gardens and a white arch that stands on the Canada-U.S. border.
peace-arch.body: Peace Arch Park is at the south end of Surrey, and the arch sits on the boundary. The gardens are handsome and the lawn works for a picnic. You can move around inside the park, but this is not an informal border crossing. Follow the park signs and do not drive into the lineup. It is a walk and a photo, not a playground. Fairhaven, on the U.S. side, requires a real border crossing.
tips: Set the navigator to the Canadian park, not the border booths.
A trip to Bellingham needs passports and legal status, plus lineup time.

whiterock-pier.summary: A long pier, a large white rock, and a whole street of seaside restaurants.
whiterock-pier.body: White Rock's waterfront has a long wooden pier. From the end you can see the water and the American shore. More sand shows at low tide. The city is named for the big white rock on the beach. Marine Drive is full of restaurants, and weekend lunch means a wait. The walk down from uptown is steep. Park at the beach with a stroller instead of pushing it down and back up. The wind is strong.
tips: The wind is harder on the pier. You will regret leaving the jacket in the car.
Beach parking circles in peak season. Come in the morning.

whiterock-museum.summary: A small museum in the old station, useful when a squall hits.
whiterock-museum.body: The White Rock Museum is in a former train station by the beach. Exhibits cover the seaside railway and the town. It is small, which makes it a half-hour shelter in the middle of a pier walk, not a destination on its own. Hours and a low admission are set by the museum, and small museums often close on Monday. Then go back to the sand.
tips: Check the open days before you make a special trip inside.
There are more restaurants than museum rooms. Eat if you are hungry.

reifel.summary: In fall and winter there are so many birds that children quiet down on their own.
reifel.body: Reifel is on an island west of Ladner, with ponds, reeds, and wooded paths. From October to February the migrants peak, and snow geese and ducks can fill the sky. You must book, and it is closed on Mondays. Admission is modest. You may bring seed only if the sanctuary allows it. Do not bring outside bread or seed. The main loop is flat enough for a stroller. There is no restaurant.
tips: Reserve on the website. Weekend spaces fill.
Wear shoes that can get dirty. Paths soften after rain. Bring or rent binoculars.

boundary.summary: A wide Boundary Bay beach. At low tide you can walk a long way, and it is good for kites.
boundary.body: Centennial Beach is on Boundary Bay in Delta. The sand is long, and the flats get very wide at low tide. Summer is for sand. Other seasons are for walking and kites. The water is shallow, but a rising tide pushes people back, so check the tide before you walk out. There is a playground and picnic space. The wind is often strong. It is free. Splashdown and the ferry terminal are in the same Tsawwassen area if you are building a summer day.
tips: Put the tide time on your phone before you walk out.
The mud is not hard ground. Stop the stroller at the edge of the sand.

deas.summary: A small river island, old houses, and a dyke that suits bikes.
deas.body: Deas Island sits between arms of the Fraser, with grass, picnics, and a few historic cottages. Paths are flat. You can see large ships. It suits a morning by the river when you do not want the beach. Cottage interiors are not open every day. Summer has shade, and fall is for looking at the river. Ladner village is the lunch connection.
tips: Navigate to the park name. Do not stop on the highway shoulder.
Families with bikes like the flat paths.

ladner.summary: Delta's small main street, with more brunch and bakeries than sights.
ladner.body: Ladner is Delta's old town. The main street has cafes, bread, and small shops. Use it as the meal stop for Reifel or Centennial Beach, not as a playground destination. There are lights at Christmas. You can walk the dock and look at boats. Give toddlers a walk and a meal, then go to the real outdoors.
tips: Weekend brunch means a wait. Bring snacks.
The bird sanctuary is still about twenty minutes from here. They are not the same parking lot.

splashdown.summary: Waterslides and pools, open only in summer.
splashdown.body: Splashdown is in Tsawwassen. It is an outdoor waterpark with a children's area and faster slides. It usually runs from late May to early September. Do not come in October. Tickets are per person and a family day is not cheap. Bring swimsuits, towels, and waterproof sunscreen. Height rules are posted at each slide. Food inside is expensive.
tips: Open days change every year. Read this year's calendar before you buy.
Younger children will spend most of the time in the shallow area. That is a normal day.

capilano.summary: The North Shore's famous bridge, with a Halloween setup in October and lights in winter.
capilano.body: The Capilano bridge crosses a canyon. The same ticket includes the treetop walk and the cliff walk. The bridge sways. Hold children and walk slowly if heights are hard, or stay on the platforms at either end. Tickets are at the expensive end for the region. B.C. residents can sometimes turn a day ticket into an annual pass. Check the rules. From early October into early November the park runs Canyon Frights, a family-leaning Halloween setup. From late November into January, Canyon Lights needs a reserved time. The deck is slippery in rain.
tips: Lynn Canyon's bridge is free if the budget is tight.
Weekend parking fills. The shuttle is easier than circling the entrance.

lynn.summary: A free suspension bridge over a deep green canyon pool.
lynn.body: The Lynn Canyon bridge is narrower than Capilano and sways more, and it is free. It is a few minutes from the ecology centre. The centre has exhibits and washrooms and keeps shorter hours than the park. Trails on both sides can be steep and full of roots. Do not take a stroller down them. The pools look swimmable. The rock is slippery and the current is fast. Do not let children enter the water or climb wet stone. The forest is especially good in fall.
tips: If heights are a problem, skip the bridge. The canyon is still the visit.
Summer weekend parking fills. Arrive in the morning.

grouse.summary: A gondola up the mountain over Vancouver. Ski in winter. Zip lines and a lumberjack show in summer.
grouse.body: Grouse takes you to the top restaurant and viewing decks by gondola. On a clear day the city and the water are below. Winter is for skiing and skating. Other seasons have walks, a lumberjack show, and paid adventure add-ons. The Grouse Grind is a steep staircase. It is not for toddlers or strollers. Ride the gondola if you do not want to climb. The top is windy and at least one layer colder than the city. Tickets are expensive. Wildlife talk times depend on the day.
tips: The Grind is not the family route. The gondola is.
If cloud wraps the summit, the view is gone. Consider another day.

hatchery.summary: Free salmon viewing. From September to November the fish are behind the glass.
hatchery.body: The hatchery is run by the federal fisheries department and does not charge admission. In the run, adult salmon climb the ladder, and indoors you can see them through glass. In other months you can see fry tanks and exhibits. It is less dramatic, but still a short, clear lesson. It connects on foot to Cleveland Dam. Do not feed the fish or climb down to the riverbed.
tips: October is the peak. Come early on weekends.
Walk up to the dam afterward. You do not need a second parking lot.

cleveland.summary: The dam drops the river into the canyon. The sound and the height stop children in their tracks.
cleveland.body: Cleveland Dam holds back the Capilano River and forms the reservoir above. You can walk the top and watch the spill. It is windy. Railings are high, and toddlers still need a hand. There is picnic grass on the reservoir side. It is free and usually done with the hatchery. Do not climb the railings or play in closed areas below the dam.
tips: The amount of water depends on the season. It is not always postcard-full.
Bring a hat and a jacket. The dam is colder than the parking lot.

deepcove.summary: A small dock, a cone, and a village facing the snowy mountains.
deepcove.body: Deep Cove is the bay village at the east end of North Vancouver. The dock looks at boats and kayakers, and the park grass is for toddlers. The ice-cream shop is the finish line for many families. The village is small and takes about an hour to walk. The rest of the time, sit and look at the water. Quarry Rock starts here, and that is a separate hike. Do not assume a toddler is going up. Weekend parking is tight.
tips: Do not feed the geese and ducks bread.
Add Quarry Rock only if you want the hike. Otherwise stay at the dock.

quarry.summary: One of the easier North Shore viewpoints. It still has a steep section.
quarry.body: Quarry Rock starts in Deep Cove. One way takes about thirty minutes to an hour, depending on stops. The end is a large rock looking over Indian Arm and the mountains. The edge is not fully fenced. Keep children well back. The trail has steps and roots. A stroller cannot do it, and it is slippery after rain. Weekend midday feels like a shopping street. This is not a toddler outing.
tips: Do not step close to the edge for a photo.
Bring water, and buy a cone back in Deep Cove.

maplewood.summary: A small city farm with goats, cows, and feeding times you can plan around.
maplewood.body: Maplewood Farm is run by the District of North Vancouver parks department. It is small, complete, and built for children. You may see milking, wool, or feeding, depending on that day's sheet. Hours are about 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Admission is low. Spring has young animals, and December has holiday activities. The ground is mud and grass. This is the outing where a toddler is happier than at a suspension bridge.
tips: Pick up the day's schedule at the gate so you do not miss milking.
Food at the farm is simple. Lonsdale can be the real meal.

lonsdale.summary: Ride the boat across the harbour and get off at a market and a play corner.
lonsdale.body: The SeaBus is the show. Children stand at the window and watch container ships while downtown moves away. Lonsdale Quay has an indoor market, food, and a children's area. You can ride over and back without buying anything else. The Shipyards outside have water play and steps, better in summer. The wind is strong.
tips: The SeaBus uses a regular transit fare, with a lower child's fare.
Boats are about every fifteen minutes. Leave the play area before you need one.

seymour.summary: Ski and snowshoe in winter. Walk high trails and see the ocean in summer.
seymour.body: Mount Seymour is the quieter of the three North Shore ski hills. Winter has a ski school and snowshoe trails, which suits a first time on snow. Tickets and rentals are extra. Summer and fall trails in the provincial park look over the city and the water. Weather changes fast up high, so bring a jacket. In snow season the car needs legal winter tires. Do not drive up without them. Keep toddlers in a coached area rather than untracked deep snow.
tips: Check that the road is open before you leave.
Pick Seymour or Grouse, not both, in the same week.

rice-lake.summary: An easy lakeside path where you can watch people fish.
rice-lake.body: Rice Lake is in the Lower Seymour conservation area. The loop is short and gentle, and it suits a family better than Quarry Rock. People fish from the dock. The forest looks good in October. There is no food. You can leave the hatchery for another week so every weekend is not another look at water. Bikes are allowed. Keep them apart from people walking.
tips: The reserve sometimes charges vehicles or limits hours. Read the gate sign.
Watching someone fish does not require a licence. Fishing does.

cates.summary: A bay park with a beach, lawn, and canoes.
cates.body: Cates Park, also called Whey-ah-Wichen, is on Indian Arm. The beach is small and friendly, the grass is for picnics, and you can see boats toward Deep Cove. This is also a Coast Salish place. Read the signs with children. The water is cold even in summer. Facilities feel more like a park than the Deep Cove dock. A stroller is fine on the grass and the main path.
tips: Respect what the cultural signs ask. Do not climb poles or memorials.
Deep Cove is across the arm. You can do both, or pick one.

lighthouse.summary: Old forest leading to a working lighthouse, with the sea beyond.
lighthouse.body: Lighthouse Park keeps a large stand of old forest. Trails run over roots and rock, so a stroller cannot enter. The lighthouse is about twenty to forty minutes in. You cannot climb it. The point is the trees and the view. Shore rocks are slippery, and waves can reach higher than they look. Keep children off the wet edge. Weekend parking is limited. October is quiet, dark, and green.
tips: Wear shoes that grip.
There is no food. Eat in Dundarave or Ambleside.

whytecliff.summary: A rocky shore and water clear enough to see the bottom.
whytecliff.body: Whytecliff is west of Horseshoe Bay. It is a rock park, not a sand beach. The water is clear, and in summer people snorkel in the marked area. Rocks are slippery and waves rise suddenly, so hold toddlers. There is grass for a picnic. Ferries pass nearby, which children like. A stroller can reach the viewpoint and should not go down onto the rocks.
tips: Do not run on wet stone.
Horseshoe Bay fish and chips can be the meal afterward.

ambleside.summary: West Vancouver's flattest seawall, with Stanley Park across the water.
ambleside.body: The Ambleside seawall runs from the park toward Dundarave. It is flat, long, and faces English Bay. Strollers and bikes both fit. Stay in the right lane. The beach is at the park end, and summer is for sand. You can see the Lions Gate Bridge and downtown. It is free and windy. It is the day for a family that wants the water and does not want a climb.
tips: Evening is when the bridge lights come on.
Eat in Dundarave. Do not expect shops on the seawall.

cypress.summary: West Vancouver's ski hill. Ski in winter, and walk the high country in other seasons.
cypress.body: Cypress was a 2010 Olympic snow venue. Winter is for family skiing and snowshoeing. Tickets and rentals are a large spend. For a first time, take a lesson rather than starting on a steep run. The snow road is steep and needs legal winter tires or chains. Drive it slowly. Summer and fall trails in the provincial park are beautiful and cold. You do not need Grouse, Seymour, and Cypress in one week.
tips: Check whether the road is open. Snow can close it suddenly.
A toddler snow lesson is safer than parents teaching it themselves.

horseshoe.summary: Watch ferries turn, eat fish and chips, or sail from here to Bowen Island.
horseshoe.body: Horseshoe Bay is the ferry port for Nanaimo, the Sunshine Coast, and Bowen Island. Even if you do not board, watching a large ship turn is the sight. Fish and chips by the terminal is the classic West Vancouver family meal. The village is small. Weekends are busy with people and cars. If you are going to Bowen, check the sailing first, then decide whether to eat before or after.
tips: If you are not taking the ferry, do not drive into the waiting lanes.
The wind is strong. An outdoor table needs a jacket.

whyte-lake.summary: A short climb into a quiet lake in the forest.
whyte-lake.body: The Whyte Lake trail leaves from near Horseshoe Bay and climbs for about forty-five minutes one way. The lake is not a swimming pool. It is surrounded by forest. It suits school-age children who can walk a hill, not a stroller or a child who still needs to be carried. It is muddy after rain. Weekends are busy, but the walking is easier than the rocks at Lighthouse Park. Bring water. There is no shop at the lake.
tips: Return the way you came.
Pair it with fish and chips in Horseshoe Bay.

lafarge.summary: A lake beside the SkyTrain station, with a fountain, a boardwalk, and holiday lights.
lafarge.body: Lafarge Lake is at the end of the Millennium Line. The loop is flat and very easy with a stroller. Summer has fountain times, and December has a light display that is better at night. Swimming is not the plan. It suits a family without a car, or a one-hour outing. The mall is next door if the rain starts.
tips: The light festival is crowded. SkyTrain is easier than driving.
The fountain does not run all day. Check the city notice.

mundy.summary: A lake and a playground inside a large wood, with an outdoor pool in summer.
mundy.body: Mundy is Coquitlam's big community park, with forest, a lake, and play equipment. The outdoor pool is summer only. Trails can be a short loop. It suits a local afternoon, and it is also a less crowded park if you are coming from Vancouver. A stroller belongs on the paved paths.
tips: Treat the pool as closed in October.
In the woods, stay on a marked loop.

minnekhada.summary: Marsh and a high lookout. In fall you can see the whole valley.
minnekhada.body: Minnekhada has low marsh trails and a stone lookout above. The high point looks over the Pitt River and the mountains, and October is especially good. The steps mean the stroller stays below. The low boardwalk is easier. Weekends are popular. Food and washrooms are limited, so use the facilities at the entrance.
tips: If you want an easy walk, stay on the marsh loop.
The lookout is windy. Bring a jacket.

colony.summary: Old farmland turned into riverbank grass. Good for bikes and birds.
colony.body: Colony Farm is a flat regional park. The paths are long and straight, so a bike is more fun than a hike. You can see birds and the mountains. There is no playground noise. Spring and fall light is good. A stroller is fine. It suits a family that wants children on bikes without going into the mountains.
tips: The valley wind is colder than the map suggests.
There is little shade. Wear a hat in summer.

crunch.summary: A long outdoor staircase up the hillside, for teens who already like hills.
crunch.body: The Coquitlam Crunch is a long set of outdoor stairs that locals use for exercise. It is not a children's playground, and toddlers should not try it. A teen who wants a challenge can climb partway and come back down. You do not have to reach the top. There is no shade. Bring water. It is free. For a view with less effort, use Burnaby Mountain or Minnekhada.
tips: The steps are slippery in rain.
Knees and shoes matter more than speed.

rocky.summary: A playground, a pier, and a shore path, all reachable by SkyTrain.
rocky.body: Rocky Point is Port Moody's main park: a large playground, picnics, a pier, and a shore for watching boats. A stroller is easy. Summer has stage events. The Shoreline Trail can continue in either direction. Food is in the brewery district. With very small children, pick daytime and a restaurant with seats. This is the simplest waterfront in the Tri-Cities.
tips: The playground is on the city side. The pier is on the other.
Claim a barbecue spot early on weekend afternoons.

belcarra.summary: A picnic bay with a pier, a beach, and trails into the forest.
belcarra.body: Belcarra is on the peninsula north of Port Moody, facing Indian Arm. There is grass, a pier, and shore trails of different difficulty. Summer is the classic picnic, and the parking lot fills, so have a backup. The water is cold. Fall is quieter, with mushrooms and leaves, and the weather can change. A stroller can use the main grass and should not go into the woods.
tips: On summer weekends, arrive before 9 a.m. or the lot may be full.
The park asks you to take garbage out. Do that.

buntzen.summary: A lake in the mountains for swimming, a picnic, and a loop walk.
buntzen.body: Buntzen Lake is managed by the power company and is one of the family's swimming lakes in summer. The water is cold even in August, so be ready for children who only stand in the shallows. Lifeguard areas and hours depend on that year's notice. Do not swim far when there is no lifeguard. The full loop is long. With toddlers, stay near the beach. Peak parking costs money and often fills. October is for walking, not swimming.
tips: Do not hand supervision to a float toy.
Sasamat Lake is the nearby backup, and it fills too.

sasamat.summary: A smaller swimming lake than Buntzen. In summer you still need to arrive early.
sasamat.body: Sasamat Lake, around White Pine Beach, warms a little faster than the ocean, which is why summer weekends are extremely popular. Parking fills early. The shallows suit children who can walk, and an adult still needs to be within arm's reach. In spring and fall, treat it as a forest lake for a walk. Facilities are at park level. Bring food.
tips: If there is no legal space, do not invent one on the roadside.
Pick this or a Belcarra picnic, and leave time to walk.

poco-trail.summary: A river loop around Port Coquitlam. Bike families come back to it.
poco-trail.body: The Traboulay trail follows the rivers around the city. The full loop is long, so families usually ride or walk one piece. The surface is flat. You can see the river, boats, and farms. There is no single climax. It suits a family that already has bikes and wants a path that is not a mountain. A stroller can use the paved parts. Summer is exposed.
tips: Start at an entrance with a washroom, such as Citadel Landing.
You do not need to finish the loop.

citadel.summary: A riverside playground and a dock. The best pause on the river trail.
citadel.body: Citadel Landing has play equipment, grass, and a river view, and it is the most natural place to stop on the Traboulay trail. Toddlers have somewhere to play while adults watch the water. Summer sometimes brings a market or an event, not every week. It is a community-scale stop and a relaxed Port Coquitlam half day. You do not need to drive into the mountains.
tips: It is better combined with a piece of the river trail.
The river reflects. Use sunscreen.

queens.summary: A century-old park: a playground, a tiny pet corner, and a large lawn.
queens.body: Queen's Park is New Westminster's old park, with tall trees. The children's area has a playground and a very small animal corner with goats and birds. That corner keeps shorter hours than the park. A gym and sports fields are next door. It suits half a day, not a long hike. A stroller is easy. The lawn is at its best from May to August.
tips: The animal corner is not a zoo. Lower the expectation. Toddlers still like it.
The quay can be the other half of the day.

quay.summary: Step off the SkyTrain and you are at the river, a market, a boardwalk, and large boats.
quay.body: New Westminster station opens onto the Fraser. The quay market has food, and the boardwalk looks at tugs and barges. Pier Park next door has play and grass. The indoor market can hide you from rain, but it has fewer shops than Granville Island, so put the expectation on the river. The quay has lights at Christmas. Stroller access is good.
tips: Look at the boats before you decide to eat in the market.
This is the easiest riverfront to reach without a car.

irving.summary: An 1860s wooden house, part of the New Westminster Museum.
irving.body: Irving House is one of the oldest houses in British Columbia still on its original site, run by the New Westminster Museum. Open hours are limited, often a few hours on weekends, and on weekdays you may only see the outside. The rooms are Victorian, which suits a child who wants the story. Admission is free or low. Check the museum. The hill is steep. If it is closed, give the time to Queen's Park.
tips: Check the open day first.
Say in advance that the objects inside cannot be touched.

fort-langley.summary: A wooden fur-trade fort, with a blacksmith and interpreters in old clothes.
fort-langley.body: Fort Langley is a national historic site. You can walk the yard, the wooden buildings, and the river path. Interpreters demonstrate work of the time, and children can join small tasks. Admission is per person and modest. If an upper level is under repair, the ground floor and yard still work. Fort Langley village next door has cafes and shops for lunch. There are evening events at Christmas.
tips: From Highway 1, take exit 66 north, through the village, to the end of Mavis Avenue.
The Greater Vancouver Zoo is the same direction if you want both in one day.

campbell.summary: Big grass and forest in the valley. Birds in spring, picnics in fall.
campbell.body: Campbell Valley is a regional park with a visitor centre, flat paths, and longer forest loops. You sometimes see horses. The space is large, which suits a family that wants to leave the mall. A stroller can use the main paths. There is no ocean. Do it on a different week from Fort Langley so you are not rushing two parking lots.
tips: The visitor centre closes earlier than the park.
Spring birding brings more people. The paths stay wide.

derby.summary: River woods and a swimming bar. Locals come here to cool off in summer.
derby.body: Derby Reach is on the Fraser east of Fort Langley. People swim at Edgewater Bar in summer. The current and the depth change, so children stay in the shallows with an adult watching. The park also has historic ground and trails. Brae Island nearby has camping and more river path. This is a free picnic place, not a lifeguarded pool. In October, walk. Do not plan to swim.
tips: The river is not a pool, and there is no lifeguard.
Mosquitoes are serious on midsummer evenings.

flight.summary: A hangar of old aircraft beside a small airport, close enough to touch.
flight.body: The Canadian Museum of Flight is at Langley Airport. The hangar holds historic planes, and on some days you can watch light aircraft outside. It is small. School-age children who like machines will stay. A toddler may want grass after half an hour. Admission is modest. Check open days. A small museum often has a closed day. You can pair it with Fort Langley, but both are indoor-and-listen visits, so put a meal and some running room between them.
tips: Check the open day first.
Watching a takeoff from outside the fence can excite a toddler more than the hangar.

gvzoo.summary: The zoo you can drive to from Greater Vancouver, open through the late afternoon.
gvzoo.body: The Greater Vancouver Zoo is in Aldergrove. The animals include rescues and exhibit animals. Paths are outside, so a rainy day still means walking outdoors. It is open daily from about 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., with last entry around 5 p.m. Special events can close it early. Admission is in the middle range. The site is flat and a stroller helps. Food is simple. Bring water in summer. In winter the animals move less, and so do the crowds.
tips: Check the website for an early close.
Fort Langley is the same direction. Both in one day is a lot for a toddler. The zoo alone is enough.

aldergrove-lake.summary: A regional park with a lake. Picnic in summer, walk in other seasons.
aldergrove-lake.body: Aldergrove Regional Park has a lake, forest, and picnic grass. Summer is a local cooling-off spot. The water is cold and the facilities are simple. Other seasons suit a short walk. If the zoo is already the plan, this can be a one-hour stop on the way. It does not need to be its own long drive. Take garbage out.
tips: If you are doing the zoo the same day, see the animals first and eat by the lake.
Do not swim far on a day without a lifeguard.

golden-ears.summary: Alouette Lake: swimming, a beach, and the Golden Ears behind it.
golden-ears.body: For families, the heart of Golden Ears is Alouette Lake. Summer has a beach. The water is cold and the depth changes, so stay in shallows you trust. In peak season the provincial park often needs a day pass, and the lot fills. If it is full, do not force it that day. The shore suits a picnic. The waterfall is a different trail. October is for walking the shore, not swimming.
tips: Read the BC Parks day-pass and parking rules before you leave.
Gold Creek Falls is the backup. Do not try to finish both.

gold-creek.summary: A walk along the creek to a waterfall, a bit more effort than the lakeshore.
gold-creek.body: Gold Creek Falls starts from the north parking lot in Golden Ears. The creekside trail is about two hours return, with roots and a little up and down. The falls are not huge, but the walk suits school-age children. A stroller does not. It is the same park as the lake beach and not the same short path. Do not assume you will swim after the falls. After rain, stop at the viewpoint. The rock is slippery.
tips: Return the way you came.
A park day pass may still be required.

kanaka.summary: A canyon, a fish ladder, and a waterfall. Salmon in the fall.
kanaka.body: Kanaka Creek Regional Park follows one stream, with a cliff path, a waterfall, and a fish ladder. From September to November you may see salmon, not on every section. There are steps. A stroller suits only some entrances. It is wilder than the Capilano hatchery. It suits a family that has already done the city fish ladder and wants a different creek.
tips: Pick one entrance and a short loop. Do not try to walk the whole park.
Wet wood is slippery.

grant-narrows.summary: Birds and mountains. You can also rent a boat, and that is a separate skill.
grant-narrows.body: Grant Narrows is where the Pitt River meets Pitt Lake. The viewing tower and the dyke are free. Birds are best in spring and fall, and the mountains are right to the north. Walking the shore suits the whole family. Canoe rental into Widgeon Creek needs paddling experience, life jackets, and a look at the wind and the water level. Beginners should not put a toddler in a boat because it looks popular. Food is limited.
tips: The default outing is birdwatching from shore, not paddling.
The road north is a dead end. You come back the same way.

pitt-polder.summary: In winter, snow geese can land in the fields and turn them white.
pitt-polder.body: Pitt Polder is farmland and dyke. In a big winter, snow geese are spectacular. They do not fill the same week every year. An empty field is not a failure. The birds move. The road is narrow. Park only where it is allowed, and do not block farm traffic. Children like binoculars and counting. There is no playground. Grant Narrows can be the same day, from the fields to the lake on one road.
tips: Use binoculars or a long lens. Do not chase birds into the fields.
December to February is the best hope. October is only the start.

mill-lake.summary: A downtown lake and fountain, useful for stretching legs on the way.
mill-lake.body: Mill Lake is in central Abbotsford, with a path, play equipment, and a fountain. It is not the end of a long hike. It is a civilized stop between a farm and a play park. A stroller is easy. Summer has community events. If the day is already Castle Fun Park or pumpkins, give the lake thirty minutes to an hour.
tips: Parking beside the park is easier on weekends than a beach lot.
You do not need a second Abbotsford park.

maan.summary: Berries in summer, pumpkins in October, and lights in December.
maan.body: Maan Farms changes with the season: strawberries and blueberries in summer, pumpkins and a cornfield in September and October, and often holiday lights at the end of the year. Not every ordinary weekday has activities. Sometimes only the shop is open. Read what the farm is doing that week before you buy an activity ticket. The ground is dirt and grass. Toddler rides such as a small tractor change from year to year.
tips: Mid-October may still have pumpkins, and late October may not. Check the site.
Weekend afternoons have the longest lines.

castle.summary: Mini golf, go-karts, and an arcade. Half of it still works in the rain.
castle.body: Castle Fun Park puts mini golf, go-karts, bumper cars, and an arcade together beside Highway 1 in Abbotsford. The indoor part works in rain. Golf depends on the weather. You pay by activity, and a family that does everything spends more than a small amount. Go-karts have a height rule. It suits school-age children and teens. Toddlers can do only part of it. Do not stack it tightly against a seasonal visit to Maan Farms.
tips: Ask which activities are indoors that day.
If a child is not tall enough, switch to mini golf instead of arguing at the kart window.

cascade.summary: A short walk to a waterfall. The water is biggest after rain.
cascade.body: The Cascade Falls trail is not long, but it has slope and rock. The falls look best after rain. Stop at the viewpoint. Do not climb the wet rock of the falls. It suits children who can already walk a trail, not a stroller. There is no shop. You can split the day with Mission's river park, or come for the falls and go home.
tips: The day after rain can be better than walking in the rain. The water is still high, and the path is less slick.
Wear shoes with a tread.

mission-park.summary: Lawn, a view, and the roofline of Westminster Abbey.
mission-park.body: The park is on a Mission hillside above the Fraser. The grass is large enough for a kite and a picnic. You can see the Benedictine abbey on the hill. The abbey is not a playground. Look from a distance, and follow quiet and visiting rules if you go in. The park is free and stroller-friendly. The view is worth the drive on a clear day. In fog it is only a lawn.
tips: If the abbey is open to visitors, dress neatly and keep voices down.
The wind is strong. Use a covered picnic box.

rolley.summary: A small, quiet provincial-park lake for families who are tired of crowded beaches.
rolley.body: Rolley Lake is smaller than Alouette Lake, with a shore path and picnics. In summer you can play in the shallows. It does not have the lifeguard density of a city pool, so an adult stays. Fall is good for walking. A provincial day pass may be required. This is the quiet choice. There is no carousel and no fish and chips.
tips: Read the BC Parks day-pass rules.
The waterfall on the same day is too much. Pick one.

cultus.summary: The valley lake that feels most like a holiday. Swim in summer, walk the shore in other seasons.
cultus.body: Cultus Lake is relatively warm and is the centre of a Chilliwack summer. The public beach, the provincial park campground, and the waterpark are three different things. The beach is free or low-cost, and peak parking is hard. The water still needs watching. October is for walking and looking at the mountains. Swimming season is mostly over by Labour Day. The highway jams on Friday afternoons.
tips: The waterpark and the beach have different tickets and different closing dates.
A packed lunch is calmer than hunting for a restaurant at the lake.

cultus-water.summary: A large outdoor waterpark in British Columbia, open from June to early September.
cultus-water.body: The waterpark has a family raft slide, a children's castle, and faster slides. The 2026 season started on June weekends, went daily from late June, and ended on September 7. Do not show up in October. Tickets are a large spend. Bring sunscreen and swimsuits. Height decides what you can ride. Shade cabanas can be reserved and go early.
tips: Confirm the season before you buy a same-day ticket online.
Younger children may spend the whole day in the children's area. That is a full visit.

vedder.summary: A long path along the river. In fall there are people fishing, and walkers can stay too.
vedder.body: The Vedder River trail is flat and long. Ride or push a stroller for a while and turn around. The riverbed is wide, and on clear fall days you can watch people fish. Do not let children walk to the fast water. There is no single landmark. It suits a family that needs to burn energy without a climb. The lake is in the same direction and can be combined, but both the lake and the river will make the day too long.
tips: Start at a parking lot that has a washroom.
River stones move. Watch the water from the path.

heron.summary: A boardwalk and a bird blind. Herons are busiest in spring.
heron.body: The reserve has wetland, trails, and a nature centre. Great blue herons are most active in the spring nesting season. Other months still work for birds and the boardwalk. The centre keeps shorter hours than the trails. A stroller can use the main boards. This is a quiet outing. The Vedder River is in the same city. Pick one.
tips: Keep voices down or the birds leave.
If the centre is closed, the trails are still open.

shannon.summary: The easiest waterfall on the Sea to Sky Highway. It is a few minutes' walk.
shannon.body: Shannon Falls is a very short walk from the parking lot. The paved path can take a stroller to the main viewpoint. The falls are tall, and after rain the spray wets your clothes. The trail above gets steep. The viewpoint is enough for toddlers. The provincial park may charge a day pass. This is the most sensible stop between the gondola and the Chief. Do not skip it.
tips: The viewpoint is slippery.
The Sea to Sky Gondola is a few minutes north. Do the free falls first.

gondola.summary: A cabin ride above Howe Sound. At the top you can take the suspension bridge or just look.
gondola.body: The Sea to Sky Gondola climbs from the highway to a summit deck over Howe Sound. Tickets are expensive. There are trails and a suspension bridge at the top. If heights are a problem, the main deck is already enough. The summit restaurant is pricey. Snacks are allowed according to the operator's rules. The top is colder and windier than the bottom. In winter there can be snow. Wear shoes that grip.
tips: If the cloud is low, the gondola may still run and the view may be white. Consider another day.
Shannon Falls is just south, and it is free.

chief.summary: A steep granite mountain, only for teens and adults who already hike.
chief.body: The Stawamus Chief is the big rock wall beside the highway. Even the first peak is a continuous steep climb, with stone steps and chains. It is not a resort trail. Do not take toddlers. Families without hiking experience should not treat it as a viewpoint. Bring water, food, and shoes that grip, and come down early in the afternoon. Turn back if the weather turns. The gondola is the other way to see the same water.
tips: This is not a backup for a stroller or a toddler.
Day-pass and parking rules are on the BC Parks page.

railway.summary: A train museum where you can climb into cars. The Royal Hudson is kept here.
railway.body: The railway heritage park is an outdoor collection of trains, and children can board some of the cars. Whether the Royal Hudson steam engine is on display, or moving, depends on the museum. Do not expect it to run every visit. The site is large. Days with the small riding train are the best, so check the time first. Part of the collection is in an indoor shed. Admission is in the middle range. A toddler who loves trains may like this more than a waterfall.
tips: See whether the mini train is running that day.
The falls, the gondola, and the trains on one day is too much. The trains can be their own trip.

britannia-mine.summary: Ride a mine cart into an old copper mine, and keep the helmet on.
britannia-mine.body: The mine museum is at Britannia Beach on the Sea to Sky Highway. The ticket includes the surface exhibits and a section underground. The tunnel is cool even in summer, so bring a layer. Helmets are provided. Stay with the guide and do not wander into a tunnel. Children usually prefer the cart to the panels. Hours and tour times are on the website. It pairs with Shannon Falls on the way home.
tips: Wear closed shoes. There is water in the tunnel.
If a child is afraid of the dark, look at photos before deciding to go in.

whistler-village.summary: A walking village: squares, a candy shop, and the place where you decide whether to go up the mountain.
whistler-village.body: Whistler Village is car-free and suits a stroller between the squares. Winter is full of skiers. Summer is mountain bikers and hikers. You can use the village without a gondola ticket: look at the squares, eat one expensive meal, and let children run by the public art. The ride up is another ticket. A day trip from Vancouver is long. Count the time in the car for a toddler. Winter tires must be legal.
tips: Leave snacks in the car. Village prices are high.
If you only have half a day, stay in the village and skip the gondola.

peak2peak.summary: A gondola between two mountains, with a deep valley underneath.
peak2peak.body: The Peak 2 Peak links Whistler Mountain and Blackcomb. Some cabins have a glass floor. If heights are a problem, choose a solid floor. The view through the windows is the same. This is the most expensive ticket on this site. In winter it is also ski transport. In summer and fall it is for the view and the alpine trails. The top is cold. Bad weather stops it. A toddler who hates hanging in the air does not have to go.
tips: Check the wind shutdown notice before you buy.
The glass floor is optional.

lost-lake.summary: The free choice when you are not going up the mountain: walk the lake, and swim in summer.
lost-lake.body: Lost Lake is beside Whistler Village. The path is gentle, and a stroller can use the main lakeside section. In summer the water is warmer than an alpine creek, and there is a beach. Other seasons are a forest walk. This is a real plan when you do not want a gondola ticket. In winter there is snowshoeing. Read the snow and your own experience, and do not leave the packed path.
tips: The walk from the village takes about twenty minutes.
Outside swimming season, expect a walk.

harrison-springs.summary: A public beach, a lake, and hot-spring water that requires a ticket.
harrison-springs.body: Harrison village sits at the end of the lake. The beach and the lakeside walk are free, and the wind is strong. The public hot-spring pool is a separate ticket and is the warm water, for people who do not want the cold lake. The resort's full pool complex is another, more expensive ticket. Do not mix them up. The beach sometimes has a seasonal sand-sculpture show. Food is in the village. This is a soak and a look at the lake, not a waterpark, and it can be a day trip.
tips: Separate the public springs from the resort. The prices are far apart.
The lake is cold. The springs are the reason to get in the water.

snug.summary: A half day on an island without taking a car: ride the ferry and eat something on shore.
snug.body: Snug Cove on Bowen Island is at the ferry door. You can do it without a car: the boat, the dock, a few cafes, and a short shore path. Count the sailing into the plan, and do not treat the last boat as the default. Choices on the island are limited, so bring a small snack. Weekend boats and the dock are crowded. This is the simplest way to put a child on a real ferry.
tips: Look at the return sailing before you relax.
Killarney Lake is an extra walk. Skip it if the ferry gap is short.

killarney.summary: A forest lake on the island. The walk from the dock climbs.
killarney.body: Killarney Lake is the quiet loop on Bowen Island. Walking up from the dock is too far for many toddlers and suits school-age children better. Do not treat the lake as a swimming destination. Leave at least forty-five minutes to walk back to the dock, and put the return sailing on the phone lock screen. There is no shop on the way. If the ferry gap is short, skip the lake and stay in Snug Cove.
tips: Put the return time on the lock screen.
A stroller belongs near the dock, not on the lake trail.

inner-harbour.summary: The other end of the ferry: the legislature, buskers, and a harbour where you can sit.
inner-harbour.body: The Inner Harbour puts the legislature, the museum, and the water within walking distance. The ferry is about an hour and a half each way, plus waiting, so this is a whole day, not an afternoon tea. Looking at the legislature is free. Public tours sometimes are too. Check that day. The Royal BC Museum is a separate ticket and is good, though a toddler may remember only the poles and the ocean floor. There are lights in December. Bring snacks for the car and the boat.
tips: Reserve the ferry. Weekends and holidays fill.
If you only have two hours, stay at the Inner Harbour. Do not add Butchart Gardens.

fishermans.summary: Float homes, fried fish, and a city park with a tall totem.
fishermans.body: Fisherman's Wharf is floating houses and takeout windows. Children like the decks and the search for seals, which are not guaranteed. Beacon Hill Park has a playground and a tall totem, and it reaches the shore. Both are reachable from the Inner Harbour. With a toddler, do not add Butchart Gardens. The gardens are outside the city, expensive, and slow. Fish and chips means a line.
tips: The floating dock has gaps and it moves. Hold hands.
The Beacon Hill sheep are sometimes in a pen. Read the sign and do not feed them.

othello.summary: Walk into old railway tunnels, with the river in the canyon beside you.
othello.body: The Othello Tunnels are a straight line of Kettle Valley Railway tunnels in the Coquihalla Canyon. The main path is flat, and a stroller can reach the open tunnel mouths. Inside it is colder than outside, and the ground may be wet. The river is fast. Swimming is prohibited, and so is leaving the walkway for the rocks. The park is generally open from May to October and closes in winter because of ice and rockfall. After the 2021 flood, repairs reopened the main walk. Some connecting trails may still be closed. Stay on the open section.
tips: Confirm the year's closing day at the end of October. Do not go in November.
Bring a small flashlight. The middle of a tunnel is dark.

fairhaven.summary: A red-brick old street after the border: a bookstore, chocolate, and a park by the water.
fairhaven.body: Fairhaven is Bellingham's historic district, with a bookstore, chocolate, and streets you can walk. Boulevard Park is on the water, with an old wharf. This is a cross-border trip. Everyone needs a passport and a visa, visa exemption, or other legal right to enter the United States. Weekend and holiday lineups can pass an hour. Children need documents too. Spend the time on a legal crossing, not on rushing the sight.
tips: If the documents are not ready, go to White Rock. It is the same piece of water.
The lineup exists on the way back too. Do not book dinner in Vancouver.

boulevard.summary: A boardwalk, play structures made of big logs, and a lawn facing the water.
boulevard.body: Boulevard Park is on the Bellingham waterfront, with a boardwalk and driftwood play that children usually prefer to shopping. It can share one border crossing with Fairhaven. You still have to enter legally first. The park is free. The weather is like White Rock, and the wind is strong. If the border used up the day, do this park and turn around.
tips: Pick Fairhaven or this park as the main stop, and let the other be on the way.
Wet wood is slippery.
